title: Fire & Ice
subtitle: The 1976 season was not just a championship battle; it was a philosophical war between James Hunt and Niki Lauda.

content.text: Lauda calculated risk with a pencil; Hunt calculated pleasure with a cigarette. In 1976, the paddock felt like a courtroom. Ferrari's tribal court had already exiled Lauda once; McLaren's garage ran on cold mathematics. The cars were loud, but the verdicts were louder.
On Sunday mornings, Hunt wore chaos like a suit. Lauda wore discipline. Their laps were the same sentence written in two handwritings.
At the Nürburgring, the track bit back. Steel met fire. Lauda's return six weeks later was not heroic in the Hollywood sense—it was a negotiation with pain, a handshake with mortality.
The title did not crown the faster man; it crowned the framework. Hunt won the points. Lauda won the argument that bravery is not stupidity. The season wrote itself into F1's bones.
